title: Dioscorides, De Materia Medica

confidence.note: No document dates the book. It is placed by his mention of Laecanius Bassus, presumed to be the consul of 64 CE, by a mention in Erotian, a Hippocratic commentator of the Neronian age (if that name is not a later insertion), and by Galen's later use of it. The text itself survives, so its contents and long afterlife are not in doubt.

place: Anazarbus, Cilicia (southern Turkey), and travels across the Roman world
people: Pedanius Dioscorides (fl. c. 50–70 CE), Greek physician and pharmacologist
Anicia Juliana, daughter of the emperor Olybrius, for whom the Vienna copy was made
summary: A Greek doctor's plain catalogue of some 600 plants stayed a leading drug authority in Europe and the Islamic world for around 1,600 years.
body: Pedanius Dioscorides came from Anazarbus in Cilicia, in what is now southern Turkey. In the letter that opens his book he says that he led a “soldier-like life”, which let him learn medicines at first hand. His *De materia medica* (“On medical materials”), written in Greek in five books, probably between about 50 and 70 CE, covers more than 600 plants, 35 animal products and 90 minerals in roughly 827 entries, in plain language and with little medical theory: how to recognize and prepare each substance, and what it is good for.

Few books have lasted so long. Copyists rearranged it and added to it; it was in Latin by the sixth century and was translated into Arabic in the ninth, with corrections by Hunayn ibn Ishaq. Around 512 a lavishly illustrated copy, its entries re-sorted alphabetically, was made in Constantinople for the noblewoman Anicia Juliana. Now in the Austrian National Library and known as the Vienna Dioscurides, it is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Printed editions multiplied in the Renaissance, above all Mattioli's of 1554. A 2010 comparison of later European drug lists found that the 19th-century Spanish pharmacopoeia still shared almost three-fifths of its simple remedies with Dioscorides.

myth.tradition: Dioscorides was an army surgeon who served the emperor Nero and gathered his plants on campaign.
myth.record: He says only that he led a “soldier-like life”. Historians infer service as an army physician from that phrase and his travels, but no source states it, and the link to Nero is a later inference.

links.note: Galen drew on Dioscorides' work, which helps date the book.

title: Soranus on childbirth

confidence.note: His dates come from two short entries in the Byzantine Suda, placing him under Trajan and Hadrian, which details in his own text support. The Gynecology itself survives in Greek, so what he taught is well known.

people: Soranus of Ephesus (fl. 98–138 CE), physician of the Methodist school
summary: A Roman-era doctor wrote antiquity's great manual for midwives, and wanted them literate, calm and trained in drugs and surgery.
body: Soranus was born at Ephesus, studied at Alexandria and practised in Rome under the emperors Trajan and Hadrian (98–138 CE), a leading figure of the Methodist school. His *Gynecology*, written chiefly for midwives, covers menstruation, contraception, pregnancy, normal and difficult births, and the care of infants. He wanted a midwife literate, calm in danger, discreet and trained in diet, surgery and drugs, and he rejected the common view that she must have borne children herself. He also describes turning a badly placed baby so it could be delivered feet first. Medieval readers knew him largely through Latin versions by Caelius Aurelianus and Mustio.

links.note: He knew Herophilus's dissections of the uterus.

title: Aqueducts, sewers and army hospitals

confidence.note: Frontinus dates Rome's first aqueduct to 441 years after the city's founding (312 BCE), and the buildings are well documented. Whether they made Romans healthier is less certain: parasite studies suggest little benefit, and how the army hospitals were staffed is reconstructed from scattered inscriptions.

people: Appius Claudius Caecus (censor 312 BCE), builder of the first aqueduct
Sextus Julius Frontinus, water commissioner of Rome under Nerva
summary: Rome piped in clean water, built sewers, latrines and army hospitals, and still crawled with worms and lice.
body: For 441 years after its founding, wrote Sextus Julius Frontinus, Rome made do with water from the Tiber, wells and springs. Then, in 312 BCE by modern reckoning, the censor Appius Claudius brought in the first aqueduct. When the emperor Nerva made Frontinus water commissioner, he called it an office concerning "the health and even the safety of the City." Across the empire Romans built multi-seat public latrines with washing facilities, sewers, fountains and bathhouses. The army built hospitals, *valetudinaria*, inside its fortresses to a standard plan; at Inchtuthil in Scotland the hospital was the largest finished building on the site, though its staffing is pieced together from inscriptions.

Whether all this made people healthier is another matter. In 2017 Piers Mitchell gathered parasite evidence from Roman latrines, burials, fossilized feces, combs and textiles. Whipworm, roundworm and dysentery-causing *Entamoeba* became gradually more common under Rome, not less, and at York lice and fleas turned up in Roman, Viking and medieval layers in similar numbers. Warm, rarely changed bathwater may have spread worms, and fish sauce traded in sealed jars may have spread fish tapeworm. Roman sanitation, Mitchell concluded, probably made people smell better rather than live healthier.

myth.tradition: Roman aqueducts, sewers and baths made Romans far healthier than the peoples they conquered.
myth.record: Archaeological parasite evidence shows intestinal worms and lice did not decline under Roman rule and some increased; any health benefit of Roman sanitation remains unproven.

links.note: A Christian institution for the sick, centuries after the first army hospitals.

title: Galen of Pergamon

confidence.note: Galen's career is known mostly from his own voluminous writings, which date his birth to 129 (one reference work gives 131) and his main works to the 160s–90s; the year of his death is uncertain, c. 200 by tradition but perhaps a decade later. That he dissected animals rather than humans, and that his authority lasted into the 16th century, is not disputed.

people: Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 200 CE), physician and philosopher
Marcus Aurelius (ruled 161–180), emperor and Galen's patron
Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), anatomist who exposed Galen's errors
summary: Galen tied off a live pig's spinal cord to show where the soul's ruling part sits, and his animal-based anatomy dominated medicine for well over a thousand years.
body: Galen was born in 129 CE into the elite of Pergamon, a Greek city near the coast of Roman Asia, the son of an architect. After his father died he spent years studying with leading teachers in Smyrna, Corinth and Alexandria, where anatomy was still taught but dissection was limited to animals. In 157 he took a post as doctor to the gladiators of Pergamon, and in the early 160s he moved to Rome. There he won patients, rivals and the favor of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, who took him on as court physician.

He was among the most prolific writers of antiquity. His works fill 21 volumes of about 1,000 pages each in the standard Greek edition, more than four million words, and a few survive only in Arabic, Syriac, Hebrew or Latin. He revered Hippocrates and Plato and presented his own views as consistent with theirs, building a system that ran from the elements hot, cold, wet and dry, through the uniform tissues, to the organs, and that placed the soul's powers in brain, heart and liver. He was a ferocious polemicist, rarely content to state a view without demolishing someone else's.

Galen also tested ideas on living animals. In one famous experiment he tied off the spinal cord of a live pig to show that the brain was the seat of the soul's ruling part. But because human dissection was not available to him, much of his human anatomy was really animal anatomy, taken largely from monkeys.

His influence was enormous and long. Greek, Roman and Arabic physicians treated his books as authoritative, and their standing reached a peak in the Middle Ages. In 1543 Andreas Vesalius, working from human bodies at Padua, publish his *Fabrica* and show that Galen, still the principal authority on anatomy, had made many errors by trusting animals.

links.note: Galen systematized Hippocratic humoral theory.

title: The Antonine Plague

confidence.note: Ancient writers clearly attest epidemic disease from the 160s to the 180s, but few describe symptoms, so it is unclear whether one disease is meant. The smallpox diagnosis rests on a handful of descriptions, notably Galen's, and has no genetic support; death-toll estimates depend on it.

place: Roman Empire, from the eastern frontier to Rome and the Rhine
people: Lucius Verus, co-emperor whose returning army was blamed
Galen (129–c. 200), physician who described the disease
summary: An epidemic swept the Roman Empire under Marcus Aurelius. It is usually called smallpox, but that diagnosis is now seriously doubted.
body: From the mid-160s CE a pestilence spread through the Roman Empire. Later Roman histories said Lucius Verus seemed to bring the pestilence home from the war in the east, and told of a soldier who cut open a golden casket in a Babylonian temple and released a deadly vapor. They describe the dead being removed from Rome in carts. Galen recorded an ulcerated, scarring rash, and modern historians long diagnosed smallpox; one classic estimate put the dead at 7–10 million. Recent genetic work casts doubt on smallpox existing in recognizable form so early, and by 2022 no ancient DNA from the epidemic had been found.

myth.tradition: The Antonine Plague was the first great smallpox epidemic and killed a large share of the empire.
myth.record: Smallpox is a modern retrospective diagnosis with no genetic confirmation, now seriously questioned, and published death tolls such as 7–10 million were built on that diagnosis.

links.note: Galen's descriptions are the main medical evidence.
The next great Roman pandemic, this time confirmed by DNA.

title: The Basileias and the birth of the hospital

confidence.note: Basil's own letter and Gregory of Nazianzus's funeral speech prove the institution existed. The traditional dates of c. 370–372 rest on a visit by Valens that only a later writer, Theodoret, links to it, and Caner argues the letter may be from the mid-370s. Whether it was a general hospital or chiefly a leprosarium is debated.

people: Basil of Caesarea (330–379), bishop and founder
Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil's friend, who described it
summary: A 4th-century bishop built a 'new city' for the sick and poor outside Caesarea. Was it the first hospital, or a leper colony?
body: Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370, built a charitable institution just outside the city walls, traditionally dated to about 372. Some in the city objected. Basil asked the provincial governor in a letter what harm there could be in a place to lodge strangers, "both for those who are on a journey and for those who require medical treatment on account of sickness", with physicians, transport and escorts. Theodoret, writing in the fifth century, says the emperor Valens gave land to support Basil's work. After Basil's death his friend Gregory of Nazianzus urged people to visit "the new city", where disease was regarded "in a religious light". It outlived its founder and became known as the Basileias, Basil's Place.

It is often called the first hospital, where Christian charity and medical care for strangers met under one roof, and historians have pictured a multipurpose complex for the sick, the poor, travelers and lepers. In 2018 the historian Daniel Caner argued that the sources point to something narrower: a monastic leprosarium, where monks and lepers lived together and lepers were the central, perhaps the only, objects of care. Either way it evidently inspired similar facilities in early Byzantium.

myth.tradition: Basil of Caesarea founded the world's first hospital, a general infirmary open to all the sick.
myth.record: His institution offered medical care, but the sources may describe a leper refuge rather than a general hospital, and calling it 'first' depends on how a hospital is defined.

title: The Plague of Justinian

confidence.note: Procopius and other contemporaries place the first outbreak precisely, and ancient DNA has confirmed the cause as Yersinia pestis. How many people died, and whether it changed the course of history, is argued between 'maximalist' historians and a revisionist challenge led by Mordechai and colleagues.

place: Pelusium (Egypt), Constantinople, and the Mediterranean world to Britain
people: Procopius of Caesarea, historian and eyewitness in Constantinople
Justinian I, emperor after whom the plague is named
summary: The first documented bubonic plague pandemic struck in 541. DNA proves the culprit; the death toll is still fiercely argued.
body: In 541 CE a disease broke out at Pelusium in Egypt. It reached Constantinople in 542 and by the winter of 543 had spread to North Africa, Italy, Spain and the French-German borderlands. The historian Procopius, in the capital, described painful swellings in the groin, armpits and near the ears, black pustules and vomiting of blood, and doctors cutting open the swellings of the dead to understand the disease. He claimed deaths in the city reached 5,000 a day, then 10,000 and more. Outbreaks recurred until about 750.

Ancient DNA settled the cause: *Yersinia pestis*, the bacterium of bubonic plague, was found in 6th-century graves in Bavaria, and in 2019 eight more genomes came from Britain, France, Germany and Spain. The toll is another matter. A long-standing consensus held that the plague killed a quarter to half of the Mediterranean population and helped end antiquity. In 2019 Lee Mordechai and colleagues argued that this rests on a few dramatic texts, while papyri, coins, inscriptions and pollen records show more continuity than collapse.

myth.tradition: The Plague of Justinian killed a quarter to a half of the Roman world and brought antiquity to an end.
myth.record: That figure is an estimate built mainly on a few literary accounts; other evidence suggests a smaller impact, and the true toll is unknown.

links.note: The second plague pandemic, caused by the same bacterium.
An earlier Roman pandemic of uncertain cause.
Later societies' organized response to plague.

title: The compilers: Oribasius to Paul of Aegina

confidence.note: The works survive and their authors' careers are roughly datable, though Paul of Aegina's dates are uncertain; his 19th-century translator Francis Adams, following an earlier argument, put him no earlier than about 600. How much the compilers added of their own is still debated.

place: Constantinople, Alexandria and the eastern Mediterranean
people: Oribasius (c. 325–403), physician to the emperor Julian
Aetius of Amida (c. 502–575), court physician under Justinian
Paul of Aegina (7th century), compiler of the Epitome in seven books
summary: Late antique doctors boiled Greek medicine down into handbooks, preserving lost authors and feeding Arabic medicine.
body: From the 4th to the 7th century, Greek physicians condensed their predecessors into handbooks. Oribasius, physician to the emperor Julian, excerpted Galen, Rufus, Soranus and others into a 70-book medical encyclopedia, a third of which survives. Aetius of Amida, court physician under Justinian, compiled the *Tetrabiblos*, now the chief source for parts of Rufus, Soranus and others. Paul of Aegina cut it all down again into seven books, setting down, he admitted, "little of my own". Arabic authors, his 19th-century translator observed, quoted him on almost every page.

links.note: Galen was their chief authority.
Their compendia passed into Arabic medicine.
Oribasius and Aetius preserved his work.
